resources.string: How Apex works
Apex calculates its own scores from your own data. They are not Whoop, Oura, Garmin or Fitbit scores, and they are not medical measurements. Nothing here diagnoses or treats anything.
When a reading is missing, Apex shows it as missing. It never fills the gap with a guess or a population average.
Recovery
Recovery is a score from 0 to 100 that compares how your body looks this morning with your own usual range.

Heart rate variability counts most (40 percent), then resting heart rate (25 percent) and sleep (25 percent). Breathing rate and skin temperature (5 percent each) only take points away when they drift well above your usual. If you log a fatigue rating, or your recent training load is available, they join in with a small weight.

If a sensor is missing, its weight is shared out among the others, so the score still spans 0 to 100. It needs at least heart rate variability or resting heart rate. Without either, Apex shows that Recovery is calibrating or unavailable.
A score of 67 or more is labelled Peak, 34 to 66 Moderate and 0 to 33 Restorative. These labels describe your load, not your health.
Strain
Strain is a derived cardio strain on a 0 to 21 scale. It adds up how much of your day your heart spent working well above rest.

For each minute, Apex measures where your heart rate sits between your resting rate and your maximum, and weights harder minutes more heavily (the Banister training impulse). Minutes in the easiest part of the range are ignored so a day of sitting and walking does not count as training.
The total is put on a curve that rises quickly at first and flattens at the top, so the last points are hard to earn. Today\'s strain is provisional until the day ends.
Sleep

The sleep score runs from 0 to 100 and combines five parts: how long you slept against your need (35 percent), how your heart rate and heart rate variability during sleep compared with your own usual (25 percent), your deep and REM sleep compared with your own usual (15 percent), efficiency (15 percent) and how regular your sleep times are (10 percent). An ordinary night lands around 75 to 85.

Sleep need starts from about 7 hours 45 minutes, or from your own recent nights once there are enough, and adds a little after hard days and a little to repay sleep debt, to a maximum of 10 hours. If a part cannot be worked out, for example when no sleep stages were recorded, it is left out and the rest are scaled up.

Why Apex can differ from Google Health: Google\'s sleep score is proprietary and is not available from its API, so Apex cannot copy it. Apex\'s score is transparent, every part is shown, and it includes how your body recovered overnight.
Training load

Training load builds on the same daily heart-rate load that drives Strain. Acute load is a 7-day moving average and chronic load is a 28-day one. Their ratio shows whether this week is lighter or heavier than what you are used to.

A ratio of 0.80 to 1.30 is shown as the sweet spot, below 0.80 as under usual load, 1.31 to 1.49 as overreaching caution, and 1.50 and above as high fatigue risk. Research on how these bands relate to injury is mixed, so treat them as load-management guidance and not a prediction.
The ratio needs enough history, and Apex adds a caveat when history is short, your usual load is very low, or many days are missing. A day with no heart rate data counts as unknown, not as zero.
Baselines and calibration
Your baseline for a metric is the average of the 30 days before the day being scored. The day itself is left out, so a reading is never compared with an average it helped to form.

Your normal range is the baseline plus or minus one standard deviation. Heart rate variability is averaged on a log scale because it changes in proportions, so its normal range is a little wider above than below.
Apex needs at least 7 valid days before it trusts a baseline. Until then the metric is calibrating and the scores that depend on it stay locked, rather than falling back to population norms.
VO2 max
When your wearable reports a VO2 max, Apex shows that value and names the source.

Only when the wearable has not reported one, Apex can estimate it from the ratio of your maximum to your resting heart rate. That estimate is always labelled Estimated. It was studied in trained men, so it is better for following a trend than as an exact number.
Max HR
If you enter a maximum heart rate in your profile, Apex uses it.

Otherwise it uses the higher of two values: an age-based estimate (208 minus 0.7 times your age, labelled Estimated) and the highest one-minute average your wearable has recorded. Heart rate zones are set at 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90 percent of this maximum.
